sentences.text: Turnipax is an extinct genus of buttonquail that lived during the Oligocene Rupelian epoch.
The genus name Turnipax combines parts of the names of the charadriiform genus Scolopax and the turnicid genus Turnix.
Gastroliths found in T. oechslerorum suggest this bird had at least a facultatively granivorous diet.
A second species, T. oechslerorum, was described from a nearly complete skeleton missing only the head and right foot.

The type species T. dissipata was discovered near the village of Céreste-en-Luberon in France. Mayr described this species in 2000 based on a strongly dissociated skeleton from Rupelian deposits near Céreste-en-Luberon, southern France.

A second species, T. oechslerorum, was described from a nearly complete skeleton found south of Wiesloch, Germany. Mayr and Knopf named T. oechslerorum in 2007 based on an almost complete skeleton missing only the head and right foot. The species name T. oechslerorum honors Annette and Harald Oechsler for their contribution to finding the fossils.
Modern buttonquails are omnivorous, feeding on seeds, plant matter, and invertebrates while ingesting grit to aid digestion.
Mayr and Knopf (2007) proposed that Turnipax represents a stem lineage of the family Turnicidae.
Later studies classified Cerestenia as a stem Turnicidae, similar to Turnipax.
Turnipax lived during the Rupelian epoch of the Oligocene. Turnipax lived between 33.9 and 27.3 million years ago during the Rupelian stage.

The Frauenweiler fossil site where T. oechslerorum was found represents marine deposits within a clay pit. The marine deposits at the Frauenweiler site were likely formed during a transgression caused by rifting activities.
The Rauenberg Lagerstätte is similar to the Oligocene Luberon area where T. dissipata was discovered.
